t: How To Love Being A Teacher
q: More is being asked of us now than at any time in my 25 years of teaching. Stress is at an all-time high.
And yet, there is a small band of teachers who have figured out how to fight back.
They’ve figured out how to love being a teacher. (And not just try to convince themselves they do.)

The book is a culmination of my career-long quest for the single most effective and fulfilling teaching approach in existence—and not just in the classroom, but from the moment you arrive on campus until you leave for the day.
I’ve taken the traits, qualities, and practices of the happiest and most effective teachers on Earth and condensed them into 11 habits any teacher can apply and experience dramatic results.
It was important to me not just to tell you that a particular method or strategy is effective, but show you exactly why it’s effective and how you can apply it in your own classroom.
It is this: Many victims are unsure if they’re actually being bullied.
You see, bullies are good at making you think that they’re really your friend.
This underscores the importance of defining for your students—through modeling, playacting, and role-playing—what bullying looks like.
It’s a very simple test, but it’s 100% accurate in determining who is and isn’t a bully.
But what it does do is give the victim a surefire way to know if they’re being bullied. Because, if the person being asked doesn’t stop, then by definition, they’re a bully.
Furthermore, when “please stop” becomes the culture of your classroom or school it can virtually wipe out bullying behavior.

t: How to Handle A Student Who Yells At You
q: But then, out of the blue, a student stood up and accused her of favoring one team over another.
The instant you recognize—or think you recognize—a student becoming angry, your singular goal is to calm them down and avoid confrontation.

Instead, stay cool and relaxed, pretend it’s no big deal, and say “It’s okay. I understand what you’re saying. I can see how you might feel that way. I promise I’ll fix it, but let’s finish the game first.
You are under no obligation to explain yourself or your decisions to any student who speaks to you or approaches you disrespectfully —nor should you.

Any incident of brazen or continued disrespect should be met with your strongest consequence—which may include an extended time-out for elementary students or detention for high school students—plus a notification of parents.
As counterintuitive as it may seem, the less contact you have with the offending student, the less likely a similar incident will happen in the future.
The phrase “in a moment” keeps students from moving on while you’re giving directions.
It bridges the gap between knowing what to do and doing it with speed, accuracy, and confidence.
Because once you say ‘go,’ you’re handing responsibility in total over to them—with very reluctant additional support from you.
A final pause of 15-20 seconds will cause students to visualize themselves successfully doing whatever you want them to do.
This simple two-part strategy of giving directions— in a moment and when I say go —can turn distracted, bored, and daydreaming students into active and tenacious listeners.
As soon as your students think they understand what you’re asking of them, they mentally check out.
In response, it’s common for teachers to increase the volume of their voice in an effort to cut through the fog.
A better way to handle it is to utter three simple words before giving directions.
The phrase is: “In a moment.” As in, “In a moment, we’re going to begin writing a response to the day’s reading.
It keeps students from moving on mentally or physically until you’ve finished giving every last direction.
The most effective teachers use the phrase up to a dozen times a day.
Eventually, active listening will become Pavlovian in response.
